title: The Long-Term Memory Problem: Why Teaching and Learning Policies Fail
author: Carousel: Teaching, Learning, Leading
summary: A school walkthrough reveals well-written policies, strong training, and visibly aligned practice, yet when asked three-week recall questions from exercise books, almost no student can answer. The school has in-the-moment teaching strategy but almost nothing for learning over time. Long-term retrieval fails systematically because historic curriculum discourse undervalued knowledge durability, observations reward easier signals, curriculum time feels too tight, teachers avoid the depression of testing recall, and seductive quick-fixes like Do Nows substitute for real spacing strategy. The load-bearing argument is stark: if curriculum has not been coded for retrieval, scheduled with proper spacing, and reinforced through high-quality homework, nothing done in class can compensate, and outcomes looking out of line with classroom quality usually trace to this missing layer.
points: Schools routinely have strong in-the-moment teaching strategy and almost nothing for long-term consolidation, yet outcomes failures usually trace to retrieval strategy gaps, not classroom practice gaps.
Long-term learning is underobservable in the ways school culture rewards, so schools default to proxies (engagement, busyness) and miss the real signal (retrieval success over time).
Do Nows and other quick-fixes give the appearance of strategy while substituting for real spacing, thereby creating an illusion of action that hides the missing retrieval architecture.
The curriculum must be explicitly codified for retrieval, with clear spacing decisions and responsive strategies for when students struggle; without it, time investment in teaching is wasted.
Homework is the natural pressure valve for distributed retrieval but degrades into set-and-forget ritual when teachers don't engage with what students actually recall and can do.
quotes: Leaders tell me that they think the policy is good and that teachers are following it, but student outcomes don't seem to be improving, and they aren't sure why.” “It seems to be a smooth operation, with well-written policies, effective staff training, and a positive culture around professional and institutional growth. Unfortunately, the bottom line is the bottom line, and if we aren't shifting the dial on student outcomes, then however lovely our school is, something is clearly going wrong.

However well designed our lessons, however clear our explanations, however thorough our checks for understanding and however extensive our independent practice: without a clear strategy for how students are going to remember it over the long term, we are wasting our time.

In order to strengthen our students' long-term memory, we need to give them lots of opportunities to retrieve and practise their knowledge. These opportunities need to not only be extensive, but also to be appropriately spaced and spread out over time.

Professor Coe's seminal work on 'proxies for learning' taught us that when trying to establish the quality of a teacher or lesson we latch onto things that are readily observable, like student behaviour, busy-ness, and if feedback is being delivered. Whether students are learning over the long term feels more ephemeral.

Asking students questions about things you taught them and discovering that they remember nothing is difficult and frustrating, and most of us will consciously or subconsciously try to avoid getting into that situation.
When teachers 'set and forget' they therefore communicate that they don't really care what students do, so long as they do it. But if the teacher doesn't care, the students certainly won't.

If we have not adequately strategised for long-term learning, nothing we do in the class can compensate. We need to scrutinise our teaching and our leading and wonder: have we been looking in the wrong direction?” Archived from Carousel on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
